{"id": "20:50/q07", "question": "Does 'every thing' cover individuals or kinds?", "turns_on": "Whether incidental defects and the past tense limit a universal statement.", "positions": [{"id": "20:50/q07/p1", "position": "It covers every individual in its fitting rank.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī rejects restricting it because incidental defects do not undo each thing's completeness in its own rank; he cites 32:7 and 67:3 and says past tense does not establish a restriction. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows distributive generality: each receives its own creation as each rider mounts their own animal. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues unqualified wording extends guidance to everything."}, {"id": "20:50/q07/p2", "position": "It denotes kinds, or conventional generality limited to suitable recipients.", "reasons": "Some in al-Ālūsī invoke defective individuals; al-Ālūsī counters that even if many individuals do not yet exist, already existing kinds do not settle the past-tense objection. Ibn ʿĀshūr permits conventional generality; the animal-mate explanation likewise takes 'all' as abundance."}]}
{"id": "20:50/q08", "question": "To what does God guide creatures?", "turns_on": "Whether guidance is general practical direction, mating instinct, the universal movement toward an end, religious guidance, destiny, or a later faculty.", "positions": [{"id": "20:50/q08/p1", "position": "He directs each creature toward its needs, welfare and livelihood.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Qatāda and Yahyā speak of learned benefit and taking what is needed; al-Suddī and Muqātil specify pasture and food, with grain and meat differing by animal. Ibn Qutayba includes avoiding danger; Ibn ʿAbbās lists food, drink, dwelling, birth and mates. Al-Rāzī adds refining materials, preparing medicines and food, bees' hexagonal cells, and offspring finding mothers' breasts. Al-Ḥasan connects guidance to what makes a thing sound; Abū Isḥāq and al-Zajjāj include mating within the broader welfare sense. Al-Qurṭubī says general wording encompasses the explanations, and Ibn Qutayba says their senses relate."}, {"id": "20:50/q08/p2", "position": "He inspires creatures to find and approach their mates.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī, al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Qutayba stress instinctive intercourse; al-Zajjāj says males approach females without instruction. Ibn ʿAbbās adds affection, joined hearts and marriage; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr glosses knowledge of how a male approaches a female. This is included in the broader welfare reading according to Abū Isḥāq and al-Zajjāj."}, {"id": "20:50/q08/p3", "position": "He guides beings to their created ends and fullest attainable development.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī distinguishes instinct from choice and preservation from perfection; al-Burūsawī links equipment to purpose. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī defines guidance as showing or conveying a thing to its goal: innate powers produce its effects, as an embryo becomes a human; interacting systems are governance from another view. Al-Ālūsī reports natural powers in nonanimals and choice in animals, but objects that 'creation' already includes powers and this makes 'guided' metaphorical."}, {"id": "20:50/q08/p4", "position": "He grants religious guidance and a path to afterlife blessing.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī and al-Jubbāʾī pair worldly gifts with religion and eternal afterlife blessings; al-Nasafī includes happiness in the next life. Ibn Sābiṭ's four animal guidances include knowing God as Lord, mating, livelihood and fearing death. Al-Burūsawī infers all creatures know and glorify God according to their faculties, citing 17:44. Al-Iṣlāḥī adds messengers and books for humanity."}, {"id": "20:50/q08/p5", "position": "He fixes destinies and guides creatures through them without departure.", "reasons": "Some exegetes align 20:50 with 87:3 and specify decreed deeds, lifespans and provisions."}, {"id": "20:50/q08/p6", "position": "He creates cognitive and motive powers after forming bodies.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares Adam's formed body before the spirit and human developmental stages, citing 15:29 and 23:12–14. Al-Ālūsī objects that creation is broader than bodily assembly and already includes motion and perception."}, {"id": "20:50/q08/p7", "position": "He guides human beings to know His existence and unity.", "reasons": "A view reported by al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī connects dispositionally sought existence with human knowledge of God; he rejects its restriction of the verse without evidence."}]}
{"id": "20:50/q09", "question": "What does 'then' mark between giving and guiding?", "turns_on": "Whether the sequence is temporal, ranked, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "20:50/q09/p1", "position": "It marks real succession: formation precedes later guidance or powers.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī argues bodies precede cognitive and motive faculties, citing Adam's form before spirit and human stages in 15:29 and 23:12–14; Bursevī similarly says creation precedes endowment with powers. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows both temporal and ranked sequence and compares the paths shown in 90:8–10."}, {"id": "20:50/q09/p2", "position": "It marks rank or ontological order, without requiring elapsed time.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī makes the imparting of spirit majestic beside other differences. Al-Ālūsī says guidance follows creation in order of being even without time separating them. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says bodily beings' progression can also unfold in time; Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise allows both."}]}
{"id": "20:50/q10", "question": "Why say God 'gave' creation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:50/q10/p1", "position": "The verb presents creation as a bestowed blessing.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says 'gave' reminds hearers that creation is a blessing and proof of lordship. Al-Burhān says the verb suits beings whose existence lasts only a moment."}]}
{"id": "20:50/q11", "question": "What does Moses' formulation establish about the Lord?", "turns_on": "How acts of creation and guidance establish divine lordship and human response.", "positions": [{"id": "20:50/q11/p1", "position": "Creation and guidance prove one self-sufficient, powerful, knowing Lord to whom beings depend.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Rāzī infer a creator and guide from the acts; al-Rāzī cites 87:1–3 and 26:77–78, biological design, bees' hexagonal cells, and the body's reversed elemental order. Death proves powers contingent; neither humans nor parents designed them. A bodily cause regresses, so an incorporeal necessary manager acts by choice, knows, and has unlimited power. Al-Biqāʿī rejects nature and stars as explanations for differentiated creatures. Al-Bayḍāwī stresses God's self-sufficiency; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says creating entails ownership and governance, including only dependent delegated possession (3:26). Ibn ʿĀshūr includes Pharaoh under 'everything'; he knows he did not create it. Al-Iṣlāḥī cites birdsong and plants, and 87:1–3; human capacities and sciences remain God's gifts."}, {"id": "20:50/q11/p2", "position": "The created world directs the self to God through proof and obliges following guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī calls this guidance of the self by proof; al-Jishumī rejects imitation, necessity, inspiration and anthropomorphist accounts of knowing God, and says innovators lack salvation. Al-Ālūsī says Moses' method rebuts blind imitation and learning God solely from a messenger's assertion; one must hear objections to answer them, and even Pharaoh argued rather than abusing the claimant. Al-Iṣlāḥī cites 75:14–15 for inner testimony and warns that intellect and scientific achievement should not breed defiance."}]}
{"id": "20:50/q12", "question": "Why answer Pharaoh with these acts and words?", "turns_on": "Whether the distinctive wording serves proof, the immediate call to guidance, or a timeless view of creation.", "positions": [{"id": "20:50/q12/p1", "position": "The answer is concise and comprehensive and supplies proof that Pharaoh cannot claim.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and those citing him call it clear to an unbiased seeker; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Pharaoh cannot share the attributes. Al-Bayḍāwī says Pharaoh was confounded and changed subject; al-Iṣlāḥī calls the answer gentle yet cornering. Al-Ālūsī contrasts the mere title 'Lord of the worlds' with a description of origination, dependence and differing ranks; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī likewise says it supplies proof. Bursevī says the act points to its agent."}, {"id": "20:50/q12/p2", "position": "Guidance is foregrounded because Pharaoh's exchange concerns a call to guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says universal guidance particularly suits the context."}, {"id": "20:50/q12/p3", "position": "The past tense expresses ongoing, timeless creation.", "reasons": "Asad reads the grammatical past as an unceasing present."}]}
{"id": "20:50/q13", "question": "Did Pharaoh already know God?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative description presupposes Pharaoh's recognition of a creator.", "positions": [{"id": "20:50/q13/p1", "position": "He knew of God but rebelled or questioned His essence.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and some in al-Ālūsī say a relative description assumes recognition. They cite Pharaoh's acknowledgment in 17:102, opponents' inner certainty in 27:14, 28:39 as denial of resurrection, his 'who' question and 'madman' charge in 26:23,27, and his rational awareness of his origin and limited realm. Al-Ālūsī says the question may concern unknowable essence after a proof of existence, but calls the arguments disputable; the Study Quran says God's essence is inaccessible, citing 26:23–24 and 3:13,15."}, {"id": "20:50/q13/p2", "position": "He was ignorant of God in some manner.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports possibilities of denial of a maker, necessary-cause philosophy, star or idol worship, indwelling, or anthropomorphism. He says Pharaoh's claim to lordship over subjects demands their obedience, not necessarily that he created everything."}]}

{"id": "20:53/q01", "question": "How is الذي جعل لكم attached grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative continues Moses' description of his Lord or opens a divine resumption, especially in light of the later first person.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q01/p1", "position": "It is the predicate of an omitted subject, such as 'He is.'", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari lists this; Razi insists on it because the later first person is divine; Ibn Ashur takes the omitted subject to resume the Lord of 20:52. Alusi's Imam calls the divine resumption certain."}, {"id": "20:53/q01/p2", "position": "It is an adjective of 'my Lord.'", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari and others allow this; Razi and Abu Hayyan object that it makes Moses continue speaking across the later first-person verbs; al-Samin identifies the same difficulty."}, {"id": "20:53/q01/p3", "position": "It is an accusative of praise or an omitted 'I mean.'", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and others give this parse; al-Samin says it can introduce God's speech; Razi objects if it makes Moses speak onward."}]}
{"id": "20:53/q02", "question": "How is مَهْدًۭا read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted reader groups and whether the noun form better fits the context and 78:6.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q02/p1", "position": "Mahdan, without alif, with fatḥ on mīm and a still hāʾ.", "reasons": "Most Kufans, including ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī, read this here and at 43:10; Abu Hayyan adds al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa and Ibn Abi Layla; Ibn Ashur adds Khalaf. Al-Nashr calls a report from Rawḥ erroneous."}, {"id": "20:53/q02/p2", "position": "Mihādan, with alif, kasra on mīm and fatḥ on hāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir read this; the sources compare 43:10 and the unanimous alif at 78:6, though al-Baghawi cites 78:16. {"id": "20:53/q03", "question": "What do mahd and mihād mean and how are they formed?", "turns_on": "Whether the forms distinguish an action from a prepared object, form a singular and plural, or both function as verbal nouns.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q03/p1", "position": "Mihād names a spread, bed or carpet; mahd is primarily the act of preparing or spreading.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari compares farsh/firāsh; Abu Ali and al-Farisi call this clearest; al-Nahhas says mahd requires an implied 'possessing a cradle.' Al-Raghib says the prepared child's bed extends to a level place."}, {"id": "20:53/q03/p2", "position": "Mahd is itself a noun for a cradle or bed, and mihād may be its plural.", "reasons": "Al-Farisi allows the faʿl-to-fiʿāl plural; Ibn Atiyya and al-Mahdawi allow singular or plural mihād; Ibn Ashur says the plural can point to many regions; al-Alusi says each place is someone's cradle."}, {"id": "20:53/q03/p3", "position": "Both forms can function as verbal nouns or near synonyms.", "reasons": "Al-Mufaddal derives both from mahada, preparing a bed; al-Samin records this analysis; Ibn al-Jawzi says both denote a bed or spread."}]}
{"id": "20:53/q04", "question": "In what sense was the earth made a cradle?", "turns_on": "Whether the cradle image denotes present physical habitability or life's preparatory role.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q04/p1", "position": "It was spread and prepared as a settled, useful place for human life.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Yahya, Razi and others describe rest, sitting, standing, sleeping, dwelling, farming and travel; 2:22 and 71:19–20 are parallels. Biqai says most land is habitable amid mountains and rough regions; Ibn Ashur notes rare avoidable bumps."}, {"id": "20:53/q04/p2", "position": "Its comparison with a cradle points to human earthly life preparing for higher life.", "reasons": "Tabatabai compares the child raised in a cradle for a later, nobler life."}]}
{"id": "20:53/q05", "question": "What does سَلَكَ mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the local sense is opening a route or an image based on inserting something into another thing.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q05/p1", "position": "God opened, laid out and made routes passable.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and al-Thaʿlabi gloss it as opening a way; Ibn Abbas says the roads were made easy. {"id": "20:53/q06", "question": "What are the سُبُل and what do they enable?", "turns_on": "Whether the ways are physical routes alone, broader resources, or also an image of spiritual travel.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q06/p1", "position": "They are roads through the earth for travel and access to needs.", "reasons": "Qatada glosses roads; sources locate them amid mountains, valleys, plains and sand. {"id": "20:53/q09", "question": "What is meant by ٱلسَّمَآءِ?", "turns_on": "Whether 'sky' indicates the direction above, clouds or a heavenly origin.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q09/p1", "position": "It can mean the sky's direction or regions.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas says its regions; al-Alusi offers 'from its direction.'"}, {"id": "20:53/q09/p2", "position": "It can mean the heavenly sphere or the clouds, or heaven itself.", "reasons": "Bursevi says anything above may be called sky, including the sphere and clouds; al-Alusi reports a literal heavenly origin in some reports."}]}
{"id": "20:53/q10", "question": "What is the water sent down?", "turns_on": "Whether the mention stops at falling rain or extends to water sourced from it.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q10/p1", "position": "It is rain.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Baghawi, Tabrisi, Baydawi and others identify it as rainfall; Bursevi takes the indefinite wording to mean some water, and Biqai points to observable color and taste."}, {"id": "20:53/q10/p2", "position": "The rainwater also encompasses waters found in springs, rivers and seas.", "reasons": "Tabatabai links rainfall with terrestrial waters in his description of God's provision."}]}

{"id": "20:53/q12", "question": "What is the force of the shift to فَأَخْرَجْنَا?", "turns_on": "Whether the shift mainly marks divine sovereignty, renews attention, reflects Moses' state, or is identified as a formal turn.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q12/p1", "position": "The first-person plural emphasizes God's exclusive power, majesty, wisdom and command over diverse creation.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari points to 6:99, 35:27 and 27:60; Baydawi calls it a sign of power and wisdom; Alusi likens it to a great ruler speaking of a great act. {"id": "20:53/q13", "question": "What do the fāʾ and 'by it' express?", "turns_on": "Whether the fāʾ marks temporal succession or a further causal/willing relation alongside the bāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q13/p1", "position": "The fāʾ marks succession and the bāʾ links plant growth causally to water.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan identifies the water as the pronoun's antecedent; Alusi prefers succession in the fāʾ because the bāʾ already conveys causation; Tabatabai says the preposition affirms cosmic cause and effect."}, {"id": "20:53/q13/p2", "position": "The fāʾ makes divine willing follow rain, while the bāʾ links growth to water.", "reasons": "Al-Khafaji gives this analysis as reported by Alusi; Alusi finds simple succession more eloquent."}, {"id": "20:53/q13/p3", "position": "Sending down and bringing forth may stand for God's willing those acts.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this to avoid ascribing physical work to God; he also says the perfect verb confirms the act."}]}
{"id": "20:53/q14", "question": "Does water itself have a causal role in plant growth?", "turns_on": "Whether the preposition gives water divinely granted causal efficacy or only customary accompaniment.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q14/p1", "position": "God grants water properties by which growth follows, while God remains the true effective cause.", "reasons": "Razi says this does not violate Islamic principles; Alusi reports Maturidis and earlier authorities that properties work only with God's permission; Tabatabai takes 'by it' as affirming causal links."}, {"id": "20:53/q14/p2", "position": "Water has no inherent causal effect; God creates growth when water is present.", "reasons": "Razi reports earlier theologians' denial of water's effect; Alusi describes the Ashʿari reading of 'by it' as 'at it,' comparing water's quenching and fire's burning, while calling the charge against causal powers extreme."}]}
{"id": "20:53/q15", "question": "What does أَزْوَٰجًۭ mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether 'pairs' denotes associated species or actual sexual pairs.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q15/p1", "position": "It means kinds or varieties of vegetation.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and Mujahid give varieties; paired means associated or mutually resembling kinds, such as palms and grapes. {"id": "20:53/q16", "question": "What range does نَبَاتٍ have?", "turns_on": "Whether the note concerns the semantic extent of vegetation or the collective morphology of the noun.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q16/p1", "position": "It denotes vegetation broadly, including trees and stemless plants; ordinary usage may narrow it to fodder.", "reasons": "Al-Raghib defines every growing, feeding body as vegetation; Bursevi says the word can cover all growing things, including animals and humans in its widest sense."}, {"id": "20:53/q16/p2", "position": "It is a verbal or collective noun used for plants in singular and plural.", "reasons": "Razi and Nasafi say its form serves singular and plural; Ibn al-Anbari calls it collective without an ordinary singular, and Abu al-Baqa permits agreement with plural shattā."}]}

{"id": "20:53/q18", "question": "What does شَتَّىٰ modify, and how is it parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether shattā describes the kinds, collective vegetation, or functions adverbially as a circumstantial accusative.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q18/p1", "position": "It is an adjective describing azwāj, the diverse kinds.", "reasons": "Akhfash allows the reading; Abu Hayyan and Samīn prefer it, the latter for direct noun-adjective relation. Tabrisi makes min nabāt and shattā successive adjectives; Ibn al-Anbari allows 'varied varieties of plants.'"}, {"id": "20:53/q18/p2", "position": "It describes nabāt, the vegetation collectively.", "reasons": "Akhfash accepts this; al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa use nabāt as a verbal noun or collective whose form permits the plural description. {"id": "20:53/q26", "question": "What codex and writing background accompanies the reading notes?", "turns_on": "The reported history and differing scholarly rules for codex presentation.", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q26/p1", "position": "Accounts differ on the spread of writing into Mecca and Arabia.", "reasons": "Hisham al-Kalbi traces it from al-Anbar through Bishr, Harb and Sufyan, with Umar and Muawiya learning from them; another account begins with Tayy people from Baqqa, while al-Shaʿbi traces Muhajirun through Hira to al-Anbar."}, {"id": "20:53/q26/p2", "position": "Early script and codex spelling developed through scribal practice.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir calls al-maktufa the early script, credits Ibn Muqla and Ibn al-Bawwab with refinement, and says early codex word placement differences were orthographic rather than semantic; Abu Ubayd and Ibn Abi Dawud catalogued orthography."}, {"id": "20:53/q26/p3", "position": "Authorities differed on permissible codex spelling and notation.", "reasons": "Malik required the authoritative codex's orthography while others allowed spelling variation; scholars differed over vowel marks and dots. {"id": "20:54/q07", "question": "What do the signs establish?", "turns_on": "Which divine claims the created provisions are taken to demonstrate.", "positions": [{"id": "20:54/q07/p1", "position": "They show God's oneness, lordship, power, wisdom, and provision, inviting reflection and admonition.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls the food and pasture a lesson in oneness. {"id": "20:56/q03", "question": "How did God show Pharaoh the signs?", "turns_on": "Whether arayna denotes direct visual showing, imparted knowledge, or both; the timing of what Pharaoh had seen and the verb's object structure are cited.", "positions": [{"id": "20:56/q03/p1", "position": "He made Pharaoh see them directly.", "reasons": "Nahhas stresses direct sight rather than reports.
